title: Safe Execution of AI-Requested Actions
learning_outcomes: Explain distinguishing proposals from executed actions and how it connects to safe execution of ai-requested actions.
Apply authorization outside the model in the example and predict the output before running it.
Test one realistic edge case for safe execution of ai-requested actions and explain what the example does not prove.

content.intro: This lesson covers safe execution of ai-requested actions through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Use schema-constrained outputs and tool calls as a controlled application protocol. A model request is a proposal, not proof that an external action is authorized or completed.
content.why_it_matters: Distinguishing proposals from executed actions describes one part of a controlled action loop. The model may propose a step, but the application should independently validate the arguments, check the caller's permissions, enforce step/time limits, and record the actual tool result before deciding what happens next.

items.title: Authorization outside the model
items.text: Authorization outside the model is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

items.title: Human approval for consequential operations
items.text: Use human approval for consequential operations to reason about behavior under real workloads, not just a successful local example. Measure latency and cost on representative requests, define operational limits and rollback options, and test what happens when dependencies slow down or fail.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet to a local file such as lesson_example.py and run it with Python 3.11+ using `python lesson_example.py`. This is a local/static teaching example; CodeLeaf's current browser iframe previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript and is not a secure Python runner. Do not paste API credentials into the example or public source files.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and fixed sample inputs, rerun it, then change one input at a time and compare the new output with the stated contract.

content_blocks.title: Provider and version note
content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice distinguishing proposals from executed actions within safe execution of ai-requested actions: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.

summary: Safe Execution of AI-Requested Actions is one part of a larger generative AI application lifecycle.
Use explicit inputs, criteria, and reproducible examples to test the concept.
Document uncertainty, failure modes, security considerations, and version assumptions.
